true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage on view-only permission

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the fallback check is `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` — it treats the VIEW scope as sufficient for manage. An administrator who only has an all-groups permission with the `view` scope (and no manage-users role) will have canManage() return true. This is used by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (requireManage()) to authorize creating top-level groups, so a view-only admin can create (and, via the same check elsewhere, potentially modify) groups. The VIEW scope should be removed from this check; only MANAGE should satisfy canManage().
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug. GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() checks VIEW alongside MANAGE, so users with only view permission can pass the manage check. Both say VIEW should be removed from that check.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses authz resource ID instead of group ID

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the callback calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` and `granted.add(groupResource.getId())`. However, hasPermission(groupId, ...) looks the resource up with `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, and in the V2 schema the resource *name* is the group ID (set by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource), while resource.getId() is the internal authorization-resource UUID. Passing the UUID means findByName never matches the specific group resource (it silently falls back to the all-groups resource), and the returned set contains authz resource IDs rather than group IDs. This set is consumed by UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource as the UserModel.GROUPS filter and by getUsersCount, so admins whose user visibility comes from group view-members/manage-members permissions will get wrong (empty) user lists and counts. It should use `groupResource.getName()` in both places.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes and collects groupResource.getId(), the authz resource UUID, when it should use the resource name, which is the group ID. Both note that hasPermission resolves by name, so lookup falls back to the all-groups resource. Both also note the returned IDs are then used incorrectly in the user filters and counts.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-group resources created without resource type

AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() creates resources via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, ...)` and updates scopes, but never calls `resource.setType(...)` (unlike the V1 group permissions which set type "Group", and unlike init() which sets the type on the all-resources). GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() queries `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)`; per-group resources created through this path have a null type and will never be returned by that query, so group-specific view-members permissions are ignored when computing the groups with view permission.

No upgrade path for realms that already have an admin-permissions client

The Groups resource type, its all-groups resource, and the new scopes (manage-membership, manage-members, view-members) are only created in AdminPermissionsSchema.init(), which runs only when the admin-permissions client is first created for a realm. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change already have the client, so init() returns early and the "Groups" resource and group scopes never exist. In that state GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission() calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` with `resource` being null (getResourceTypeResource returns null), causing a NullPointerException on any group permission evaluation, and getOrCreateResource for a Groups resource would fail with ModelException("No scopes found."). A migration/update path for existing admin-permissions clients is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)` unconditionally. The abstract method signature in `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` was not updated (it still only declares `external_issue, user, assign=True, **kwargs` — and concrete implementations such as Jira and VSTS define `sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True)` without `**kwargs`). For any integration whose override does not accept extra keyword arguments, every outbound assignee sync will now raise `TypeError: sync_assignee_outbound() got an unexpected keyword argument 'assignment_source'`, which will retry 5 times and permanently break assignee sync for that provider. All concrete overrides need to be updated to accept (or swallow) the new kwarg before this ships.

Sync-cycle guard only applies when parsed source survives; from_dict silently returns None on malformed payloads

`AssignmentSource.from_dict` swallows `TypeError`/`ValueError` and returns `None`, and the task then calls `should_sync('outbound_assignee', None)`, which skips the same-integration check entirely. Any malformed or version-skewed payload in the queue (e.g. an older worker enqueued a dict without matching fields, or `queued` arrives as a string that later validation rejects) silently disables the cycle protection this PR adds, reintroducing the Jira assignment loop. At minimum a malformed payload should be logged; ideally an unparseable source should be treated conservatively rather than as 'no source'.

false_positives.candidate:
FixedQueuePool is created once on the factory and shared across partition assignments, breaking rebalances

In `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, the `FixedQueuePool` (with its worker threads) is created once when the factory is instantiated, and `create_with_partitions` hands that same pool to every new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. Arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` on every assignment/rebalance and `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy when partitions are revoked. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `shutdown=True` on every worker and shuts down every queue. After the first revoke, the shared pool is permanently dead: the next `create_with_partitions` will build a strategy around queues that raise `queue.ShutDown` on `put` and workers that have exited, so all messages either fail in submit (and get their offsets silently completed, dropping them) or are never processed. Additionally, each rebalance spawns a new commit thread while the pool is shared. The pool should be created per `create_with_partitions` call (or recreated after shutdown).

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the documented guarantee

`FixedQueuePool` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, so `work_queue.put(work_item)` in `submit` never blocks. The class docstring for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but messages will be read from Kafka and buffered in memory without limit; `poll()` only emits a gauge and never signals the processor to pause. If processing is slower than ingestion (exactly the slow-item scenario this PR targets), the consumer's memory grows unboundedly until OOM, and Kafka's max.poll.interval can be exceeded since submits always succeed instantly. Give the queues a bounded maxsize so `put` blocks and applies real backpressure.

Offsets are marked complete even when processing fails, committing failed messages with no DLQ

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` regardless of whether `result_processor` raised. That means a message whose processing throws is treated as successfully processed and its offset becomes committable, so the failure is permanently skipped (the uptime consumer has no DLQ configured). This directly contradicts the strategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. The same happens in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`'s exception handler, which adds and immediately completes the offset on any decode/submit error. Failed items should either be retried, routed to a DLQ, or at minimum not marked complete.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling is flaky and contradicts the implementation

The test asserts that after one message fails processing, `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. But the implementation completes the offset in a `finally` block even on failure, so both offsets 100 and 101 become committable and the background commit loop (1s interval) will commit offset 102. Whether the assertion passes depends purely on whether the commit thread fires within the ~2.2s polling window, making the test racy; and when it does pass, it is only because the commit thread hasn't run yet, not because failures actually prevent commits. The test should either assert the actual behavior (failed offsets are committed) or the implementation should be fixed and the test made deterministic by controlling the commit loop.

OffsetTracker state for revoked partitions is never cleaned up

`OffsetTracker` keeps `all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed`, and `partition_locks` entries for every partition forever, and the pool/tracker live as long as the factory (across rebalances). After a partition is revoked, its entries remain; worse, if the same partition is later re-assigned with the consumer continuing from a different offset, the stale `last_committed` for that partition is reused by `get_committable_offsets`, which can cause the new strategy's commit function to skip committing legitimately processed offsets (start = last_committed + 1 may be ahead of the new assignment's offsets, and `highest_committable` initialized to the old `last_committed` is never returned if lower, but a stale higher value would incorrectly suppress commits). There is no hook on partition revocation to reset per-partition state.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset branch slices queryset with a negative start, which Django does not support

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0 (which any caller can produce by supplying a cursor string like "<value>:-5:0", since Cursor.from_string accepts negative integers), the code executes `queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` with a negative start index. Django's QuerySet explicitly rejects negative slicing and raises AssertionError ("Negative indexing is not supported"), turning a client-supplied cursor into an unhandled 500. The comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Negative offsets should be rejected with BadPaginationError like the other paginators do.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the negative-offset branch in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result passing a negative cursor.offset as the queryset slice start when advanced features are enabled. The candidate adds detail about Django rejecting negative slicing, but it is the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate by datetime but is wired to order_by="-datetime"

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw attribute value, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value (a millisecond integer). The only caller, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, uses it with order_by="-datetime", so `value` is a datetime and math.floor() raises TypeError on the first page; even if that were fixed, build_queryset would compare the datetime column against a bare integer cursor value, producing wrong results or DB errors. DateTimePaginator exists precisely to handle this conversion. Any superuser/admin requesting the audit log with optimized_pagination=true will get a 500. The paginator should subclass/reuse DateTimePaginator's key conversion or the endpoint should not use it for datetime ordering.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor on a datetime value because the paginator is used with order_by='-datetime', and this raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
ZPOPMIN silently discards spans (possibly including the root span) once a segment exceeds 1000

The new eviction `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` drops the spans with the lowest end_timestamp_precise from the segment with no metric, log, or error. Previously, oversized segments were skipped at flush time with an error log and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric (code removed from _load_segment_data in buffer.py). Now spans are silently deleted from the segment, so downstream consumers receive truncated traces with no signal. Worse, because scores are end timestamps, the root span often finishes last... but a long-running root that ended early relative to children can be evicted while the span-buf:hrs flag stays set, so the segment is flushed on the fast root-timeout path with its root span missing and is_segment recomputed at flush time as false for every span. At minimum this needs a metric/log and a decision about protecting the root span.

Eviction threshold hardcoded to 1000, desynced from configurable max_segment_spans (default 1001)

The Lua script caps segment size at a hardcoded 1000, while SpansBuffer keeps the configurable `max_segment_spans` parameter (default 1001) which is now dead code after the removal of the span-count check in _load_segment_data. Operators who tuned max_segment_spans will silently get a different limit, and the two values disagree (Lua evicts down to 1000, the Python default says 1001), so a segment can be capped at 1000 spans even though configuration says 1001 are allowed. Either pass the limit into the script as an ARGV or remove the unused parameter.

Redirect-follow loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without migration or justification

The redirect resolution loop was lowered from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`. Existing segments in Redis can already have redirect chains deeper than 1000 (created while the 10k limit was in effect); for those traces, lookups now stop after 1000 hops, so new spans are written to a new span-buf:s: set keyed at the truncated chain end instead of merging with the real segment. That splits one trace into two separately flushed segments (duplicated/partial segments downstream). The removed comment explicitly acknowledged this tradeoff at 10k; the change needs either a migration/drain plan or a comment and metric for the hit-limit case.

No test covers the new zset eviction-at-1000 behavior or its interplay with flush

The PR changes segment storage from sets to sorted sets and adds eviction of spans beyond 1000 in add-buffer.lua, but the added test lines only thread end_timestamp_precise through existing tests. There is no test that (a) inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment and asserts which spans survive eviction, (b) verifies behavior when the evicted span is the root/is_segment span, or (c) checks that eviction interacts correctly with the queue timeout. Given the silent data loss this introduces, the eviction semantics should be pinned down by tests.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses Python's unstable hash(), breaking caching and invalidation across processes

The cache key is built with `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` for tuples/strings is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED randomization), so different gunicorn/uwsgi workers — and the same worker after a restart — produce different keys for the identical project set. Consequences: (1) the 60-second cache is almost never shared between workers, so the claimed performance optimization does not work; (2) worse, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67) computes the key the same way, so a process handling an allowlist change will delete a key that no other process ever reads, making invalidation silently useless. Additionally, `hash()` collisions across different project-id sets can cause one organization's cached eligibility to be applied to a different set of projects, which is a data-integrity risk (wrong counts served). Use a deterministic key, e.g. `':'.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))` or an md5/sha digest.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate raises the same problem as the golden comment. Python's hash() is non-deterministic across processes, so cache keys won't match between workers and invalidation fails. Both recommend a deterministic serialization of the project IDs instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` closes over the endpoint-level `dataset`, but the query actually runs against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-widget split path (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `discover` and a synthesized query like `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`, or with `scoped_dataset` for transaction-like widgets, while eligibility is still decided from the original request dataset. This means a widget originally on the errors dataset that is rerouted to a transaction/discover query can still get `count()` rewritten to `upsampled_count()` (wrong counts for non-error events), and conversely an errors-only discover subquery can fail the `_is_error_focused_query` check because the raw request query lacks `event.type:error`, so no upsampling is applied where it should be. The scoped dataset (and the effective query string) should be passed to the eligibility check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset, so upsampling can be wrong in the dashboard split path. The candidate also adds related consequences of this mismatch, but the core issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Substring match on 'event.type:error' mis-classifies negated or quoted queries as error-focused

`_is_error_focused_query` does `if "event.type:error" in query` on the raw lowercased query string. This returns True for queries like `!event.type:error` (explicitly excluding errors) or `message:"event.type:error"` (the string inside a quoted value). In those cases the discover query is not restricted to error events, yet `count()` will be rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`, producing wrong (under)counts for transactions/other event types. The check should parse the query with the search grammar (or at minimum check that the token isn't negated/quoted) rather than doing a naive substring test.

upsampled_count registered as a public function without private=True

The new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` is added to the discover function converter without `private=True`, unlike the neighboring internal-only functions in the same mapping which are marked `private=True`. This exposes `upsampled_count()` as a user-queryable aggregate in the public Discover query API: any user can append it to a query and get `sum(sample_weight)` on arbitrary data where `sample_weight` is null or meaningless, returning misleading numbers. Since this function is only meant to be injected server-side by the error-upsampling path, it should be marked `private=True`.

Accidentally committed git submodule pointing at the base commit

The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink (subproject commit a5d290951..., which is exactly the PR's base commit). This looks like a local clone of the repo that was accidentally `git add`ed. It will create a broken submodule entry (no `.gitmodules` URL) in the tree and should be removed from the PR.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache takes precedence over fresh grants, extending wrongful denials after permission changes

In Check, the permDenialCache is consulted before anything else and short-circuits with Allowed=false. Once a denial is cached (line 154), a user who is subsequently granted the permission (e.g. an admin adds them to a team/role, or a folder permission is created) will still be denied for up to shortCacheTTL (30s), and unlike the allow path there is no DB fallback for denial hits — even a fresh DB query showing the grant is never performed. This asymmetry means the very problem this PR fixes for grants (stale allow/deny after change) now also applies to denials with no re-query escape hatch. Consider falling through to a DB re-check when a denial entry exists but the permission grant may have changed, or at least documenting/acknowledging the up-to-30s denial stickiness, and keying the TTL shorter for denials.

Denial cache keyed on raw subject UID while permission cache uses resolved UID, causing duplicate/inconsistent entries

The denial cache key is built from checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw identifier from the request subject and may be either a numeric user ID or a UID (GetUserIdentifiers explicitly handles both forms). The permission cache, by contrast, is keyed on the resolved userIdentifiers.UID. The same user queried via 'user:123' vs 'user:<uid>' will produce two independent denial entries, and a denial cached under one form will not be hit when the same user is queried under the other form, defeating the fast-deny path and making behavior inconsistent. Resolve the UID (as getCachedIdentityPermissions already does) before building the denial key.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth state compared with non-constant-time == and state is the static pipeline signature

The OAuth `state` check in OAuthLoginView.dispatch uses `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`, a plain string comparison rather than a constant-time compare (e.g. hmac.compare_digest), and the state value is simply the pipeline signature, which is reused as the Redis session key identifier and is not a single-use nonce. This weakens the CSRF protection the OAuth state parameter is meant to provide (timing side channel and replayability of the same state value across retries of the same pipeline). Consider generating a random one-time nonce, storing it in pipeline state, and comparing with hmac.compare_digest.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says the state is the static pipeline signature rather than a single-use random nonce, and recommends generating a random one-time nonce. That is the same issue as the golden comment. The timing-comparison point is extra.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError on integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] for integrations created without sender info

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when an Integration row already exists for the installation_id but has no OrganizationIntegration, the code checks `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin cache does not honor organization invalidations, unlike getByOrganization

In getForLogin, the only staleness check is `isInvalid(cacheKey)` on the realm+mode login key. The analogous cached query method getByOrganization (line 173) additionally checks `isInvalid(orgId)` because organization-level changes (org update, org removal, IDP link/unlink performed through the organization APIs) register invalidations under the organization id, not under IDP cache keys. Any IDP link/unlink or org removal that does not route through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update() (and therefore never triggers registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate) will leave the cached getForLogin lists stale: e.g. after an organization is removed its formerly-linked IDPs become realm-level login IDPs, but the cached REALM_ONLY list will not contain them and the ORG_ONLY/ALL lists may still reference them, until some unrelated IDP change happens to invalidate the login keys. The method should also consult the organization invalidation (or register login-cache invalidation from the organization provider) before serving cached results.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions reads the feature flag but always returns false

The new helper computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false in every branch, so the feature-flag check is dead code and the flag's value is never actually consulted. Since the intent of this PR is to unconditionally disable SQL expressions, this is functionally correct, but the leftover flag evaluation is misleading: a future maintainer may 'fix' the inverted logic (returning `enabled`) and unknowingly re-enable the vulnerable DuckDB code path. The function should simply `return false` (or the call site should hard-code the error) with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264 so the disable cannot be accidentally reverted.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same code problem: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, so the flag check is dead code. The candidate reads this as intentional and the golden calls it flawed logic. The underlying issue they identify is still the same.

false_positives.candidate:
User-facing error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading

When a user submits a SQL expression, the reader now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The message should state that SQL expressions are disabled, e.g. "SQL expressions are disabled in this version of Grafana".

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

SQLite ID list built with quadratic string concatenation

false_positives.candidate:
unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, skipping reason tracking and MessageBus notification

The action mutates `tu.notification_level` directly and calls `tu.save!` instead of `TopicUser.change`. `TopicUser.change` sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` (:user_changed) and publishes `notification_level_change` over MessageBus. Bypassing it means (a) other open browser tabs/devices never learn of the change in real time, and (b) because `notifications_reason_id` stays null, auto-track logic (`TopicUser.auto_track` and the auto-track branch in `update_last_read`) can silently flip the user's level back to tracking the next time they read the topic, undoing the unsubscribe.

State-changing unsubscribe performed on a plain GET request

The new `GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe` route immediately mutes/regularizes the topic for the logged-in user as a side effect of rendering the page. GET links in emails are routinely pre-fetched by mail scanners and link-protection services (e.g. Outlook SafeLinks, corporate proxies), so a user can have a topic muted without ever clicking anything. Unsubscribe links should land on a confirmation page and perform the state change via POST/PUT (as the site's existing email unsubscribe flow does with a key + POST), or at minimum only apply the change after explicit user confirmation.

unsubscribe_url ignores relative_root / subfolder installs incorrectly in redirect

`unsubscribe_url` is built as `"#{url}/unsubscribe"` where `url` uses `Discourse.base_url` (no `Discourse.base_uri` path handling issue for emails, which is fine), but in `TopicsController#unsubscribe` it is also used for the 301 slug-redirect (`redirect_to @topic_view.topic.unsubscribe_url`). Redirecting to the absolute URL is acceptable, but the redirect condition `(!request.format.json? && params[:slug].blank?)` combined with this absolute URL means the no-slug route `/t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` issues a redirect on every email click before doing the work — harmless but an extra hop; more importantly the JSON-format branch never redirects even when the slug is wrong, so the state change happens on mismatched-slug API calls.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Script uses macOS-only sed syntax and fails on Linux

`sed -i '' -E ...` is the BSD/macOS form of in-place sed; on GNU/Linux `sed -i ''` treats the empty string as a file name and the script errors out. Since this helper script is committed for the whole team, developers on Linux cannot use it to update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm file.bak`) or detect the platform. Additionally, `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's working directory, so running the script from anywhere other than its own directory silently creates/edits the wrong .env file.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same problem: `sed -i ''` is macOS/BSD-only syntax and fails on Linux. The candidate's extra note about the ENV_FILE path doesn't change that match.

false_positives.candidate:
Null credentialIds from delegation credentials break the connectedCalendars query

`connectedCalendars.map((cal) => cal.credentialId)` collects credential IDs and passes them straight into `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, which runs `prisma.calendarCache.groupBy({ where: { credentialId: { in: credentialIds } } })`. For delegation credentials, connected calendar entries have `credentialId: null` (they are identified by `delegationCredentialId` instead — the UI in this same PR handles that case). Passing `null` inside the `in` array for the non-nullable Int field `credentialId` causes a PrismaClientValidationError, so the entire `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query fails for any user who has a delegation-credential calendar connection. The IDs should be filtered (e.g. `.filter((id): id is number => typeof id === 'number')`) before querying.

Cache deletion does not invalidate connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status in the UI

The `deleteCacheMutation` only calls `showToast` and the optional `onSuccess` prop on success, but unlike the `disconnectMutation` in the same file it never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. After the user deletes the cache, the dropdown continues to show the old "Last updated" timestamp and keeps offering "Delete cached data" until a full refetch happens (and the query is configured with `refetchOnWindowFocus: false` in the wrapper). Add `await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` (as done for the disconnect mutation) so the cache status disappears immediately after deletion.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Slot end computed from slotStartTime, breaking working-hours check

In the new working-hours check inside checkIfIsAvailable, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is a copy-paste of the `start` line — it should use slotEndTime. As a result, `end > workingHour.endTime` can never be true when start is inside the working hours, so a slot that starts within working hours but ends after the end of the host's working day is treated as inside working hours and remains bookable, cutting into time the host has marked unavailable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the end time is computed from slotStartTime when it should use slotEndTime.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
dayjs objects compared with === always evaluates to false

In checkIfIsAvailable, the condition `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two distinct dayjs object references with `===`, which is always false. This branch was meant to detect a blocked-day override (where start equals end, i.e. the host marked the whole day unavailable). Because the check never fires, the callback falls through and returns undefined; find() then yields nothing, but dateOverrideExist was already set to true, so `if (dateOverrideExist) return true` makes every slot on that day bookable — the exact opposite of the intended behavior. A fixed host who uses a date override to block a whole day on a round-robin event will still be shown as available. Use `.isSame()` to compare the two instants.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: comparing dayjs objects with === checks references, so it is always false. Both also recommend .isSame() as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours minutes compared against slot's UTC wall clock

In the new working-hours check, `slotStartTime` is `time.utc()` and `start`/`end` are computed from `slotStartTime.hour()` — i.e. minutes since midnight UTC. `workingHour.startTime`/`endTime`, however, are minutes since midnight in the organizer's (schedule) timezone, as produced by getUserAvailability/getWorkingHours. Comparing the two directly only works when the organizer is in UTC; for any other timezone the check accepts or rejects slots at shifted times. For example an organizer with 9:00–17:00 IST availability (240–690 minutes UTC) compared against a slot's UTC wall clock will pass/fail on the wrong boundary, so fixed-host slots can be shown outside their actual working hours or wrongly hidden.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount-based deletion in deleteMany is not scoped to SMS method or unscheduled reminders

The new OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` deletes WorkflowReminder rows of any method (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) and any scheduled state, unlike the first branch which is constrained to `method: SMS`. Today only this SMS cron increments retryCount so the impact is latent, but the schema field is on the shared WorkflowReminder model — as soon as any other code path (e.g., the parallel scheduleEmailReminders cron or WhatsApp scheduling) uses retryCount, this job will silently delete those reminders, including ones already successfully scheduled with a Twilio referenceId. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and arguably `scheduled: false`) to the retry-count deletion clause.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: the retryCount > 1 OR clause in the deleteMany lacks a method: SMS filter, so it deletes non-SMS reminders. The candidate proposes the same fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders with empty message or missing sendTo are never counted as failures and will retry forever

The retry logic only increments retryCount when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy or when an exception is thrown. But if `message` is empty or `sendTo` is null (e.g., an SMS_NUMBER step with no sendTo, or a booking with no smsReminderNumber, or a template that produces an empty message), the code skips the entire `if (message?.length && ... && sendTo)` block without incrementing retryCount. Such a reminder stays `scheduled: false` with retryCount 0 and is re-fetched by the cron job on every run until its scheduledDate passes — exactly the infinite rescheduling this PR is meant to fix, and the most common cause (missing/invalid phone number often means sendTo is absent, not a Twilio failure).

Catch block increments retryCount even when the SMS was successfully scheduled in Twilio

The try block covers both the Twilio call and the follow-up `prisma.workflowReminder.update` that marks the reminder scheduled. If Twilio scheduling succeeds but the database update fails (transient DB error), the catch handler increments retryCount while leaving `scheduled: false`. The next cron run will schedule the same SMS again in Twilio (duplicate message to the attendee), and after two such occurrences the reminder is deleted while a Twilio-scheduled SMS still exists. The retry increment should only happen when the send itself failed, or the success-path update should be in its own try/catch.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
Prisma raw queries do not support array parameters — `ANY(${teamIds})` will fail

The new SQL conditions pass JavaScript arrays directly as raw query parameters, e.g. `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ANY(${teamIds}))` and `("userId" = ANY(${uniqueUserIds}))` (also used for team scope at line 201). Prisma's raw query serialization does not support array values as bind parameters — passing an array into a `Prisma.sql` placeholder throws a serialization error at runtime (the documented workaround is `Prisma.join(...)` for IN-style clauses). Any code path that executes these conditions via `$queryRaw` (as the updated integration test does) will throw instead of returning results, so the org and team scopes are broken for actual query execution.

`findMany` method removed — breaking change for existing callers

The PR deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, changing the service's public contract from returning typed `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` rows to returning a raw `Prisma.Sql` fragment. Nothing in this PR updates callers of `InsightsBookingService.findMany`; any existing consumer will fail to compile (and would otherwise need to hand-write raw SQL against the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` table). Either keep a query method on the service or update all call sites in the same PR.

Single filter condition returned unwrapped produces operator-precedence hazard when combined

`buildFilterConditions` returns the single condition unwrapped when only one filter is present, e.g. `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` without surrounding parentheses. `getBaseConditions` wraps conditions when both auth and filters exist, but the returned filter fragment is also exposed via `getFilterConditions()` and embedded unparenthesized in the eventTypeId condition itself (line 106 lacks outer parentheses). If this fragment is ever composed with another `AND` at a level that doesn't wrap it (as `conditions.reduce` in `buildFilterConditions` does wrap, but callers composing the raw SQL themselves may not), the OR will bind incorrectly and leak rows from other event types. Add explicit parentheses around the OR clause in the eventTypeId filter, e.g. `(("eventTypeId" = ${id}) OR ("eventParentId" = ${id}))`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync-mode Zoom refresh computes expiry_date as NaN and overwrites refresh_token with placeholder

In sync mode the endpoint returns only an access token and expiry (no `expires_in`, no `refresh_token`). parseRefreshTokenResponse fills in `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` when absent, and this code then does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` (the literal string "refresh_token") and `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` where expires_in is undefined, producing NaN. Both the corrupted refresh token and NaN expiry are persisted to the credential row, permanently breaking future Zoom refreshes for that user until they reconnect.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says parseRefreshTokenResponse fills refresh_token with the literal placeholder "refresh_token" when it is missing. It says this value gets persisted and breaks future refreshes, which is the same bug as the golden comment. It also adds a NaN expiry issue, but the core issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema uses invalid computed zod keys, so every sync-mode refresh fails validation

In zod, object shape keys must be string literals. `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` evaluate to the literal keys `"[object ZodString]"` and `"[object ZodOptional]"`, not dynamic key matchers. The resulting schema therefore requires the token response to contain a property literally named `[object ZodString]` with a number value, which no real token endpoint returns. Whenever APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, every parseRefreshTokenResponse call fails with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned', breaking token refresh for Google Calendar, Office 365 Calendar, Zoom, and Salesforce in exactly the mode this PR introduces. Use z.record() or .passthrough()/catchall() instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: the computed keys [z.string().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema are invalid Zod usage. The candidate says it causes a validation failure instead of a thrown runtime error. It still points to the same code defect and the same root cause.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync-mode refresh returns a fetch Response, but code reads res.data

refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response when credential syncing is enabled (it only returns the googleapis `res` object in the non-sync branch). The code then does `const token = res?.data; googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;`. A fetch Response has no `data` property, so `token` is undefined and reading `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. It is swallowed by the catch (message isn't 'invalid_grant'), so the Google access token is silently never refreshed when credential syncing is enabled, and calendar access breaks once the stored token expires.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. In sync mode the refresh helper returns a raw fetch Response, and callers such as the Google calendar service expect res.data, which causes runtime errors. The candidate covers the Google case that the golden comment gives as its main example.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Passes credentialId as the Cal.com userId to the sync endpoint

refreshOAuthTokens' third parameter is `userId: number | null` and is sent to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Here the code passes `credentialId` (the credential row's primary key) instead of `credential.userId`. The sync endpoint will therefore receive a wrong user id and either fail to find the user's tokens or return tokens for the wrong user. The sibling zohocrm service correctly passes `credential.userId`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: refreshOAuthTokens is passed credentialId where userId is expected, which causes wrong user lookups in credential sync.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Secret comparison is not constant-time and handler lacks method/parse guards

The webhook secret is compared with a plain `!==` on header values, which is a non-constant-time comparison for a bearer-style secret; use a timing-safe comparison. Also, the handler accepts any HTTP method (GET requests will run the full credential write path), and the zod `parse` on req.body plus `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` are unguarded, so malformed payloads produce unhandled 500s instead of 4xx responses.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate raises several issues. One of them is that the zod parse on req.body is unguarded, so malformed payloads produce 500s instead of 4xx responses. That is the same problem the golden comment describes.

false_positives.candidate:
Sync-mode refresh result treated as HubspotToken but is a fetch Response

When credential syncing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response from the sync endpoint, but the code treats the result as a HubspotToken: it reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` (undefined, so expiryDate becomes NaN) and calls `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` (undefined). The NaN expiry and undefined access token are then persisted to the credential row via prisma.credential.update, corrupting the stored HubSpot credentials. The Response body is never parsed.

Sync-mode refresh response doesn't match expected Lark RefreshTokenResp shape

In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw Response from the self-hoster's endpoint, which per the PR description contains only an access token and expiry. The code then calls handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp) and reads `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, and `data.data.expires_in`. These fields don't exist on the sync response, so `data.data` is undefined and the refresh throws, making Lark calendar refresh always fail when credential syncing is enabled. The non-Lark response shape is never mapped onto LarkAuthCredentials.

Sync-mode refresh response can't satisfy webexRefreshedTokenSchema (requires refresh_token)

When credential syncing is enabled, the sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry, but the code still validates the response with webexRefreshedTokenSchema, which requires `refresh_token: z.string()` and `refresh_token_expires_in: z.number()`. The parse therefore always fails in sync mode and refreshAccessToken rejects with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned', so Webex meetings stop working as soon as the access token expires. Unlike the other apps converted in this PR, Webex was not switched to parseRefreshTokenResponse.

Webhook updates only the first matching credential; duplicates keep stale keys

The webhook looks up an existing credential with findFirst({ userId, appId }) and updates only that one row. Cal.com can legitimately have multiple credentials for the same user+app (e.g., office365video/webex/zoom callbacks historically created duplicates, and users can reconnect creating additional rows, plus there is no unique constraint on (userId, appId)). Any additional rows retain the old keys and may still be picked up by findFirst-based lookups elsewhere, so the 'source of truth' sync silently leaves stale credentials active. Consider updating all matching rows or enforcing one credential per (userId, appId).

Sync-mode MS Teams refresh yields NaN expiry_date, causing refresh loop on every call

In sync mode the endpoint returns only an access token and expiry, with no `expires_in`. The code computes `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)`, i.e. approximately Date.now(), and persists that to the credential. Since isExpired compares expiry_date < Date.now(), the token is immediately considered expired again, so every API call triggers another sync-endpoint refresh round-trip; and if the sync response's own expiry field is never mapped, the stored expiry is effectively meaningless. Map the sync response's expiry onto expiry_date instead of relying on expires_in.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder-cancellation DB writes are fire-and-forget and may never persist

The new cancellation flow relies entirely on `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` writing `cancelled: true` to the WorkflowReminder row so the cron job can cancel the SendGrid scheduled send later. But the calls are made inside `forEach` without `await` (lines 485-493), so the handler returns (and in a serverless environment the function can be frozen/terminated) before the Prisma update completes. If the `cancelled` flag is never written, the cron job will never cancel the email and the reminder is still sent — exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix. The same pattern exists in `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (requestReschedule, lines 488-494) and in the new reschedule block in `handleNewBooking.ts` (lines 966-972). These should be awaited (e.g. `await Promise.all(...)`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the async delete reminder functions are called inside forEach without await, so the cancellations may not complete and reminders can still go out. The candidate covers the rescheduling and cancellation paths, which is enough to count as the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reschedule cancels SendGrid send immediately but never deletes the WorkflowReminder row

On reschedule, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` is called with `immediateDelete: true`. In that branch (emailReminderManager.ts lines 213-223) the SendGrid cancellation is POSTed but the WorkflowReminder database row is neither deleted nor marked `cancelled`. The row stays in the DB with `scheduled: true` and `cancelled: null` until the cron's past-date `deleteMany` eventually removes it, and the SendGrid pending cancellation is created immediately even when the reminder's scheduled date is far in the future — re-introducing the SendGrid 100-pending-cancellations accumulation this PR is trying to avoid (a pending cancellation now sits there until the original send date passes). The row should be deleted after the immediate SendGrid cancel, as `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` does.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: in the immediateDelete=true branch, the SendGrid cancel happens but the WorkflowReminder DB row is never deleted, which leaves orphaned records. The candidate does not mention the omitted DELETE API call, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
One failed SendGrid cancel aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders in the batch

In the cron's cancellation loop (lines 56-73), each `client.request` is awaited inside the `for` loop and the whole block is wrapped in a single try/catch. If SendGrid returns an error for one reminder (e.g. an unknown/expired batch_id), the exception breaks out of the loop, so every later reminder in `remindersToCancel` is skipped for that run. Because successfully processed reminders are deleted while the failing one is not, a persistently failing reminder at the front of the result set will block cancellation of all other cancelled reminders every run, and those emails will still be sent. Each iteration should catch its own error (or collect promises and use `Promise.allSettled`) so one failure doesn't block the rest.

Past-due deleteMany runs before the SendGrid cancellation pass, dropping cancelled reminders without cancelling them

The handler first deletes all EMAIL reminders with `scheduledDate <= now` (lines 34-41) and only afterwards processes `cancelled: true` reminders due within the next hour. A reminder marked `cancelled` whose scheduledDate has just passed is deleted by the first query without any SendGrid cancellation being issued. SendGrid's `sendAt` delivery is not instantaneous, so there is a window where the DB row is gone but the email has not yet been dispatched — it will then be sent for a cancelled booking with no way to stop it. The cancellation pass should run before (or be excluded from) the past-date cleanup, e.g. by excluding `cancelled: true` rows from the deleteMany until after they've been cancelled at SendGrid.

Deferred cancellation only works for reminders due within 1 hour; anything later silently stays scheduled

The non-immediate path only sets `cancelled: true` and relies on the cron job, which only picks up cancelled reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour`. For any reminder scheduled further out, nothing happens at cancel time and correctness depends entirely on the cron running within the hour before the send time. If the cron endpoint is down, misconfigured, or delayed past that window (it only runs every 15 minutes and any SendGrid error aborts the run), the email is sent for a cancelled booking with no fallback. Additionally there is no alerting when the cron fails (errors are only `console.log`ed), so this failure mode is silent. At minimum the cron window should be larger than the maximum realistic cron downtime, and failures should be surfaced.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate-guest check is case-sensitive against existing attendees

`uniqueGuests` filters with `guest === attendee.email`, a case-sensitive comparison. Since the codes are short (40 bits of entropy) and the rate limiter is the only mitigation, the consumption should be atomic (e.g., conditional update inside a transaction, or re-read-and-verify within a serializable transaction).

false_positives.candidate:
Top-level import() calls execute eagerly, defeating the lazy-loading goal

Every value in the appStore object is `import("./applecalendar")` etc. evaluated at module evaluation time. As soon as anything imports `@calcom/app-store` (e.g. videoClient, getCalendar, payment handlers), all ~29 dynamic imports are kicked off immediately, so all app packages are still loaded up front — exactly what static imports did. The only thing gained is that the promises resolve asynchronously; the bundler still creates the chunks and the module loader still fetches/evaluates every app. To actually get lazy loading, the map must store thunks like `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")` and call sites must invoke the function. As written, the PR's stated purpose ('Async imports of all apps') is not achieved, and any app whose module has import-time side effects or heavy dependencies (e.g. stripe, exchange) still pays that cost on first touch of the index.

getCalendarCredentials now returns Promise-valued `calendar` without changing its contract

Inside getCalendarCredentials, `getCalendar(credential)` is called without await, so each entry now carries `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only getConnectedCalendars in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`; getCalendarCredentials is exported and used by other code paths (e.g. availability/connected-calendars callers) that expect a synchronous Calendar instance and call methods like `listCalendars()` directly. Those callers will now call methods on a Promise and crash or silently produce wrong results. The return type change should either be propagated to all consumers (make the function async and resolve calendars there) or all call sites must be audited and updated.

requestReschedule no longer waits for calendar/video event deletions before returning

The loop `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` is now fire-and-forget: the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule email and return success while the calendar/video deletions are still in flight. Previously the forEach body was synchronous and deleteEvent promises were at least initiated with a resolved calendar; now the entire deletion (including the dynamic import + getCalendar) may never complete if the serverless function is frozen after the response is sent, leaving stale events on users' calendars. Errors are also silently swallowed as unhandled rejections. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` (optionally with per-item .catch) before sending the email.

Recurring-cancellation branch uses async forEach, so apiDeletes promises pushed after Promise.all resolves are never awaited

In the recurring-event + allRemainingBookings branch, `credentials...forEach(async (credential) => { ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })` pushes deletion promises into apiDeletes asynchronously, but the code later does `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` on line 652 — by then the async forEach callbacks may not have run yet, so the pushed deletions are not included in the awaited array and may be dropped when the function returns (serverless freeze) with their errors unhandled. This existed before but is made worse because each callback now additionally awaits getCalendar. Convert the forEach to a for..of loop or collect promises with map and await them before building apiDeletes.
